newsitem.title: Malta: Europe sees Arafat-Levy meeting as Mideast breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Europe sees Arafat-Levy meeting as Mideast breakthrough.

text.p: European diplomacy brought Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy together on Wednesday in the highest level contacts in a month of crisis and violence in the Middle East.

Neither side said the meeting made progress on substance, but a spokesman for Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, who spearheaded the diplomatic efforts, said it had "broken through the psychological barrier needed to relaunch the peace process."
Both Levy and Arafat appeared to endorse this.
Levy said he had secured a promise from Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to renew security links with the Jewish state severed last month.
"He (Arafat) announced that the cooperation on security matters will be renewed," Levy told reporters after meeting Arafat during a Euro-Mediterranean conference.
Asked on his return to Palestinian-ruled Gaza if this was true, Arafat said: "I met him and I agreed...to continue on this attitude to save the peace process."
The meeting produced no timetable for resuming the peace talks which collapsed when Israel started building a Jewish settlement in disputed Arab East Jerusalem last month.
The construction sparked clashes between Palestinian stone-throwers and Israeli troops in the West Bank and a Palestinian suicide bomber killed three Israelis in Tel Aviv.
Arafat spokesman Marwan Kanafani told reporters in Malta both leaders "agreed there should be a real attempt to go back to the peace process."
Levy, speaking in Hebrew through an interpreter, said he found the Palestinians willing to speed up talks on "final status" questions -- Jerusalem, borders and refugees.
"We will continue our efforts when we return home to define the parameters for a return to negotiations," he added.

Levy left for Israel as U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy Dennis Ross launched a fresh bid on Wednesday to rescue Middle East peacemaking, going in to talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Ross was also scheduled to meet Arafat on Wednesday.

At a news conference after the EU-Mediterranean conference closed, van Mierlo, whose country is current president of the European Union, said the Arafat-Levy meeting was a clear success for the Malta meeting.
"There's still an enormous stalemate in the Middle East peace process and we are very concerned about it but they were willing to meet and talk about it," he said.

The Middle East dominated the EU-Mediterranean meeting which was supposed to assess progress since the Barcelona 1995 meeting forged a partnership between 15 European Union states and 12 Mediterranean partners. It delayed the closing ceremony for five hours.

Van Mierlo said all the parties had agreed to a political declaration -- the toughest task -- to come from the Malta meeting, but that officials were still working on the economic and social sections of a communique. The declaration would be available next week, he said.

Conference sources said the Arabs -- who include the Palestinian Authority, Syria, Lebanon, Egypt and Algeria -- wanted a reference to the state of crisis in the Middle East included in the declaration. Israel opposed this, they said.

The sources said the final statement added to the Barcelona political declaration a preamble in which the 27 expressed their deep concern about the obstacles blocking the peace process and stressing the need for a "just, comprehensive and lasting settlement" within the framework of the Madrid peace process of October 1991.
Van Mierlo also said talks between Turkish and Greek ministers on Wednesday had made progress in resolving problems they had over islands in the Aegean sea.
Turkey and Greece came close to blows in the Aegean over the occupation of one of a series of rocky islands last year.
Van Mierlo, speaking of the meeting between Turkish undersecretary Onur Oymen and Greek's Foreign Affairs minister George Papandreou, said: "We can talk in terms of a breakthrough."
